noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that transpiration is the evaporation of water from the surface of a plant
understand how the rate of transpiration is affected by changes in humidity, wind speed, temperature and light intensity

primer.text: Every leaf is quietly drying itself on purpose. Transpiration — evaporation of water vapour from the plant's surface — pulls water skyward, cools the leaf, ferries minerals and keeps cells firm. Four weather factors set its speed, and this note ranks them.

lessons.title: What Transpiration Is and Why Plants Bother
lessons.opening: Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour from a plant's surface, mainly through the stomata on the leaf underside, and it drives water uptake, cools the leaves, carries mineral ions and keeps cells turgid.
keyPoints: Water vapour evaporates from the plant's surface.
Most loss happens through stomata on the leaf underside.
The stream pulls water skyward from root to leaf.
Turgid cells stay firm, preventing wilting.

low.restatement: Leaves leak vapour on purpose; the pull waters, cools, feeds and stiffens the plant.
low.analogy: A straw: sipping at the top drags the drink up from the bottom.
low.examPointer: Reproduce the definition's opening words — evaporation of water vapour — for the mark.

medium.restatement: The evaporation sets up a continuous pull through the xylem, so the same process that loses water is also the engine that supplies it.
medium.analogy: A chimney draft: the escaping warm air is what draws fresh air in behind it.
medium.examPointer: Link turgidity to wilting explicitly: pressure lost, leaf flops.

options.text: Water vapour evaporating from the plant's surface
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The uptake of water by root hairs
options.explanation: Uptake feeds transpiration but is not it.

options.text: The transport of sugars in phloem
options.explanation: That is translocation.

options.text: The exchange of gases in leaves
options.explanation: Gas exchange shares the stomata but differs in kind.

check.stem: Where does most transpiration take place?

options.text: Through stomata, mostly on the leaf's underside
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those absorb water; they do not lose it.
Petals are not the main site.
Bark is waterproofed against loss.

check.stem: Which benefit keeps leaves from drooping?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The cuticle limits loss; turgor stops the droop.
Sugars are solutes, not the support mechanism here.
Wind would worsen drooping.

check.stem: How does transpiration cool the leaf?

options.text: Heat energy is lost from the leaves as water evaporates
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: By shading the leaf from the sun
options.explanation: Nothing shades anything.

options.text: By conducting heat to the roots
options.explanation: Conduction downward is not the mechanism.
No cold gas exists; evaporation takes heat away.

check.stem: Which mineral ions travel with the transpiration stream?

options.text: Ions such as nitrates dissolved in the rising water
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The stream carries dissolved ions.
Sugars ride the phloem.
Oxygen is not a soil mineral ion.

check.stem: State three functions transpiration serves for the plant.
check.modelAnswer: It draws water up to the leaves, cools them by evaporation, and transports mineral ions while keeping cells turgid.

check.stem: Name the pore through which a single vapour loss event occurs.
check.modelAnswer: One pore is a stoma; the plural is stomata.

check.stem: Explain why wilting follows prolonged water shortage.
check.modelAnswer: Because without enough water the cells lose turgor pressure, so the once-firm tissues can no longer hold the leaf upright.

check.stem: A gardener mists a wilting plant's leaves at noon. Explain how misting helps briefly.
check.modelAnswer: The mist raises humidity around the leaves, slowing further evaporation so the leaf loses water more slowly while the roots catch up.

lessons.title: Four Dials That Set the Rate
lessons.opening: Wind, temperature, humidity and light intensity each move the rate: moving air and warmth speed it up, humid air slows it, and bright light opens the stomata wider.
keyPoints: Wind blows vapour away, steepening the diffusion gradient.
Higher temperature gives water molecules more kinetic energy.
High humidity saturates the air outside the leaf and slows loss.
More light opens more stomata, raising the rate.
Each factor's decrease has the opposite effect.

low.restatement: Windy, warm and bright push the rate up; humid air pushes it down.
low.analogy: Drying washing on a line: a breeze, sun and dry air help; a damp, still day does not.
low.examPointer: Learn all four directions, not just two — tables quiz any cell.

medium.restatement: Every factor acts through the same physics: the concentration gradient between leaf and air, the vapour's kinetic energy, or the number of open pores.
medium.analogy: Four taps on one tank: each opens or throttles the same outflow.
medium.examPointer: For 'explain' marks, name the gradient or the stomata, not just the trend.

check.stem: How does increased wind speed affect transpiration?

options.text: It increases the rate by sweeping vapour away from the leaf
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Removal of vapour steepens the gradient, raising loss.
Air movement is one of the four factors.
Wind does not close pores directly.

check.stem: Why does higher temperature raise the transpiration rate?

options.text: Water molecules gain kinetic energy and diffuse out of the stomata more readily
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Because stomata close in the heat
options.explanation: They open with light, not close with warmth here.
Warmer air can hold more vapour; the rate still rises.
No shrinking occurs.

check.stem: What happens to transpiration when humidity increases?

options.text: The rate decreases, because the air outside the leaf holds more water molecules
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Extra outside vapour flattens the gradient.
No doubling rule exists.
Humidity is precisely one of the four dials.

check.stem: How does light intensity raise the transpiration rate?

options.text: More stomata open, so vapour diffuses out of the leaf faster
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The named mechanism is stomatal opening.
Diffusion does the moving.
No thickening happens.

check.stem: In still, dim, dry-cold conditions compared with a windy bright warm one, the rate is...

options.text: Lower on every count, since each factor's decrease works oppositely
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Higher, because still air traps vapour near the leaf
options.explanation: Trapped vapour flattens the gradient, lowering loss.
All four dials have moved against the rate.
Some evaporation continues regardless.

check.stem: List the four factors affecting transpiration rate.
check.modelAnswer: Air movement, humidity, temperature and light intensity.

check.stem: State the humidity rule and its reason.
check.modelAnswer: As humidity increases the rate decreases, because more water molecules outside the leaf weaken the diffusion gradient.

check.stem: Explain why wind and humidity act on the same underlying cause.
check.modelAnswer: Both change the concentration gradient between the leaf's interior and the surrounding air: wind steepens it by removing vapour, humidity flattens it by adding vapour.

check.stem: A greenhouse grower wants faster transpiration for a water-hungry crop. Suggest two dial settings.
check.modelAnswer: Increase air movement with fans and raise light intensity with lamps, both of which raise the rate.

glossary.definition: The evaporation of water vapour from a plant's surface, mainly via stomata.
The leaf pores through which vapour and gases pass.
Swollen firm with water, the state that keeps leaves upright.
The amount of water vapour held in the surrounding air.
